extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in Twitter / X platform history, policies, and technology
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize the platform-level policies, technical practices, moderation criteria, and legal/compliance standards used by Twitter/X as described on the page. Includes rules for advertising, verification, developer APIs, security, privacy, and content-moderation actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising bans (specific outlets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter banned specific media outlets (RT and Sputnik) from advertising on the site (October 2017) after U.S. intelligence conclusions that they had been used as vehicles for interference in the 2016 U.S. presidential election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an example of an advertising exclusion based on national-security or foreign-influence concerns; Twitter may prohibit particular advertisers if judged to have been used for political interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political advertising policy (2019 ban; 2023 reversal with criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: In October 2019 Twitter announced it would stop running political ads (effective Nov 22, 2019). The company later reversed the ban in August 2023, publishing criteria that disallow promotion of false or misleading content and require advertisers to comply with laws, with compliance being the sole responsibility of the advertiser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political ads may be subject to entire bans, later reopened under explicit rules: no false/misleading content allowed, advertisers must follow applicable laws, and advertiser compliance is enforced only against the advertiser.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climate-related advertising restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: In April 2022 Twitter announced a ban on 'misleading' advertisements that go against the scientific consensus on climate change and stated decisions would be made with the help of 'authoritative sources', including the IPCC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudication of 'misleading' climate ads is to be informed by authoritative scientific sources; the policy aims to prevent promotion of content that contradicts scientific consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertiser compliance and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When political advertising was republished (August 2023), Twitter required advertisers to comply with laws and made compliance the sole responsibility of the advertiser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform policies may require advertisers to follow legal/regulatory rules and place enforcement responsibility on the advertiser rather than the platform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coerced advertising allegations (company conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting (2025) alleged that certain companies signed advertising contracts following legal threats from platform leadership, implying non-voluntary commercial agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not a formal policy but an allegation that commercial pressure or threats influenced advertiser behavior; relevant to evaluating ethical/commercial conduct of platform leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fines and regulatory compliance (privacy & DSA)
rubrics_metrics.description: X/Twitter has been fined for non-compliance: $150 million (FTC/DOJ, May 25, 2022) for collecting contact details and using them for targeted advertising, and €120 million (European Commission, Dec 2025) for alleged non-compliance with the Digital Services Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms must comply with privacy promises and regional regulations (e.g., FTC orders, DSA); failure can trigger large fines and may lead to advertising or other commercial consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: FTC settlement — comprehensive information security program
rubrics_metrics.description: An FTC settlement (June 24, 2010) required Twitter to maintain a 'comprehensive information security program' and be independently audited biannually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory settlements can mandate concrete security governance (programs, audits) as a compliance criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security measures (2FA, bug bounty, incident response)
rubrics_metrics.description: After major breaches, Twitter introduced two-factor authentication, operated a bug bounty program, and performed incident-response actions (e.g., disabling tweeting/resetting passwords after the July 2020 hack).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good-practice security measures include offering two-factor authentication, running a bug-bounty program to surface vulnerabilities, and having rapid incident-response mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developer API rules and changes (OAuth, usage limits, paid access)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter mandated OAuth for developers (2010), introduced stricter usage limits (2012) and later ended free third-party API access (Jan 2023), moving to paid tier plans with limited access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developer platform policies may require use of certain auth standards, impose rate/usage limits, and can change access model (free → paid), affecting third-party clients and integrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovator's Patent Agreement (defensive patent use)
rubrics_metrics.description: On April 17, 2012 Twitter announced an 'Innovators Patent Agreement' obligating Twitter to use its patents only for defensive purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporate IP policy can pledge defensive-only patent use to limit offensive litigation; this is a governance/ethical commitment regarding patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-source releases and algorithmic transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter released source code for its recommendation algorithm (March 31, 2023) to increase platform transparency; subsequent updates (Jan 2026) that depend on external large language models were described as lacking transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open-sourcing algorithms is a transparency measure, but later architecture choices (e.g., dependence on external LLMs) can undermine the intended transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification eligibility and criteria (blue check / off-Twitter notability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verified accounts (blue tick) indicate contact/identity verification. In 2016 Twitter opened public verification for accounts 'if determined to be of public interest'. In November 2020, Twitter stated it verifies six types of accounts and for some categories (companies, brands, influential individuals) the existence of a Wikipedia page is a criterion for 'Off Twitter Notability'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification requires identity validation and evidence of notability; off-platform signals (like Wikipedia entries) may be used as criteria. Verification does not imply endorsement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification via paid subscription and tiered verification markers
rubrics_metrics.description: After the 2022 takeover, verification was reported to be included in paid Twitter Blue; existing verified accounts could lose status if they did not subscribe. Organization verification programs (Verified Organizations / Twitter Blue for Business) introduced purchasable organizational markers (gold check, grey checks for government).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification policy can be monetized or restructured; markers/levels (individual, official, organization) can be implemented and sold as part of paid services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official / Organizational markers policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter reimplemented an 'Official' marker (grey tick + 'Official' text) for government and commercial entities, later replaced by gold check for organizations and grey check for government/multilateral accounts; the gold check was made purchasable by organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms may differentiate account types with distinct visual markers and can make some markers available through paid organizational programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy settings and protected accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets are public by default, but users can set accounts to 'protected' which limits visibility to approved followers and restricts follower/following information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privacy controls should allow users to limit visibility of tweets and relationship information to approved followers.

rubrics_metrics.name: User-notification policy for legal requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter's stated policy is to notify users about law enforcement and governmental requests for their information unless legally prevented from doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms should inform users of government demands except when prohibited by law; this is a transparency/notification standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective country-based content removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter offered a feature allowing tweets to be removed selectively by country rather than globally; the first uses were to block specific accounts/tweets in certain jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms may implement geo-specific removals to comply with local laws while retaining content elsewhere; this is a mechanism for jurisdictional compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of images of deceased upon family request
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter stated that in certain cases it would delete pictures of people who had died upon requests from family members and 'authorized individuals'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms may honor targeted takedown requests for sensitive content involving deceased persons from authorized family or representatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-sharing choices for EEA/GDPR users
rubrics_metrics.description: In April 2020 Twitter announced users outside the EEA/UK (subject to GDPR) would no longer be allowed to opt out of sharing 'mobile app advertising measurements' to third-party partners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data-sharing opt-in/opt-out mechanisms can vary by jurisdiction; changes may limit privacy choices for certain users, with regulatory implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retweet/quote-tweet experimentation to add context
rubrics_metrics.description: In Oct 2020 Twitter temporarily encouraged users to 'add their own commentary' before retweeting by making 'quoting tweet' mandatory in an experiment to generate context; the experiment ended in Dec 2020 after limited results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Product experiments can force user flows (e.g., forcing quote tweets) to encourage contextualization, but such measures may be rolled back if ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harassment reporting and blocking mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter introduced a 'report abuse' button (Aug 2013), updated reporting and blocking policies (Dec 2014), and adopted blocking tools devised by outside activists (e.g., Randi Harper's mechanism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective harassment mitigation involves reporting tools, blocking features, and sometimes community-sourced blocking solutions; platforms should iterate and expand reporting capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust & Safety Council advisory model (composition concerns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter created a Trust & Safety Council (2016) to advise on safety policies; critics argued the council was skewed toward restriction of hate speech and lacked uncompromising anti-censorship representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advisory bodies shape safety policy but their composition affects perceived legitimacy and balance between safety and free-speech perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension/removal criteria for extremism, terrorism, and coordinated abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter suspended large numbers of accounts for promoting terrorism, extremism, and coordinating abuse (examples: bans of accounts tied to QAnon, suspension of accounts promoting terrorism). Actions included permanent suspensions, limiting reach, and enforcement against multi-account evasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy enforcement targets promotion of terrorism/extremism, coordinated campaigns (brigading), multi-account evasion, and coordinated abuse; enforcement can include suspension, limits on discoverability, and permanent removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blocking external URLs with malicious or banned content
rubrics_metrics.description: As of July 30, 2020 Twitter will block URLs in tweets that point to external websites containing malicious content (malware, phishing) as well as hate speech, violent content, child sexual exploitation, breaches of privacy, and similar banned content. Users frequently linking to such sites may have accounts suspended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms may block or strip links to external content used to bypass on-platform content restrictions; repeated linking to such sites can trigger account-level sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety Mode automated temporary restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Safety Mode (beta Sept 2021) aims to limit unwelcome interactions by automatically identifying harmful/negative engagements and temporarily preventing those authors from following, messaging, or seeing the user's tweets. The system assesses existing relationships to avoid blocking frequent interactors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated temporary measures can reduce harassment while attempting to avoid false positives by factoring in relationship strength; these systems require tuning to balance protection and false blocking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulation / spam / fake account enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter removed thousands of accounts for violating manipulation policies (e.g., Dec 2019 removal of nearly 5,929 accounts tied to a state-run operation) and identified/shut down fake accounts linked to influence operations (e.g., Iranian fake accounts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement includes investigation, attribution where possible, removal of accounts engaging in spammy or manipulative behavior, and disclosure of findings when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency labels for political candidates / authoritative labeling partnerships
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter partnered with Ballotpedia (May 2018) to add special labels verifying authenticity of political candidates running for election in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labeling candidates or authoritative accounts via third-party partnerships is a mechanism to signal authenticity and help users assess credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account metadata transparency to combat bots and malicious accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: In November 2025 X began displaying additional information on user accounts for transparency (location, history, username changes) to combat bots and malicious accounts and reveal potential foreign influence operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surface-level account metadata can be used to detect and deter inauthentic behavior; exposing history and metadata aids user and analyst evaluation of account authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and differentiation of bots (benign vs malicious)
rubrics_metrics.description: A bot is a program that can automatically tweet/retweet/follow; benign bots generate creative content or updates, whereas malicious bots inflate popularity, push irrelevant products, and spread misinformation or spam. Bots have been noted to sway elections, influence markets, and attack governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and detection efforts should distinguish benign automated accounts from malicious ones based on purpose and behavior, focusing enforcement on accounts that manipulate, deceive, or cause harm.
